transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
Congressional Republicans are meeting privately
to elect their new leadership teams.
NPR's Claudia Grisales reports these leaders will guide the
next new minority party in Congress
after Democrats won their majority control
in the midterm elections.
>> Two top House Republicans are fighting
to replace Speaker Mike Johnson as minority leader
of the incoming conference next year.
Johnson, who said he would step down after losing majority
control, is staying out of that and other leadership races,
but he applauded those running.
>> Because we have extraordinary people who stepped up to lead
in all these positions and tough decisions ahead for everybody.
>> The number two House Republican, Steve Scalise,
is running with a promise of scoring conservative wins thanks
to his broad experience in leadership.
>> He's facing off against House Judiciary Committee chairman,
Jim Jordan, who says he'll provide the kind of clarity
for a path forward that has been missing
under the current leadership team.
Claudia Grisales, NPR News, the Capitol.
>> Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is condemning impeachment
proceedings against him.
In his first news conference in six months,
Hegseth framed the impeachment effort as an indictment
against the nation's service members and their successes,
while undermining American forces, he said, in real time.
Former Pentagon spokesman, John Elliott,
called this Hegseth's signature approach.
>> Secretary Hegseth, always when he's attacked,
he hides behind the troops, and he says,
"Well, this is an attack on the troops.
This is an attack on the president."
In that news conference, he's playing to an audience of one,
and that's the president.
He's looking into the camera, he's talking over the heads
of reporters, and he is trying to impress the one person
who controls his fate, which is the president.
>> Republican Representative Thomas Massey
launched the impeachment effort over Hegseth's handling
of the Iran war and other actions.
For the first time in years, planet-warming pollution
from fossil fuels is expected to drop in 2026,
dipping by about 0.4%.
A new study by the Global Carbon Project,
which tracks global greenhouse gas emissions,
says the drop is due to the Iran war.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shalci reports from Antalya, Turkey.
>> New research shows that oil pollution saw the biggest drop,
expected to fall roughly 1.9% globally,
mainly because the conflict in Iran disrupted fuel supplies,
resulting in decreased demand.
Major emitters like China, the U.S., and the E.U.
all saw modest declines in their fossil fuel emissions.
The new research was presented at the U.N.'s annual climate
summit, known as COP 31, by an international team
of more than 140 climate scientists.
The drop may seem like good news,
but researchers warn it's mostly due to global conflict,
causing supply crunches
and not a lasting shift to green energy.
Researchers said that coal use ticked up,
driven by surging power needs in emerging economies like India.
>> You're listening to NPR.
Dinosaur bones found pretty often,
but a new study claims to have found something exceedingly
rare -- dinosaur blood.
NPR's Nate Roth reports.
>> To be clear, we're not talking about a vial
of dinosaur blood, nor even a trail of dried dino blood.
Instead, researchers say they found chemical traces
of red blood cells and tiny mineralized structures
that look like red blood cells
in a 115-million-year-old bone.
The study, published in the Proceedings
of the National Academy of Sciences,
claims to be the most compelling evidence yet of dinosaur blood.
Other researchers who were not involved in the new study
agree that the evidence is intriguing,
but they're not ready to say these structures
are actually red blood cells.
Nate Roth, NPR News.
>> Former President Joe Biden
has some strong words for President Trump.
In his new memoir, the former president writes,
"Donald Trump has deeply damaged the country and world
with an administrative that is determined," he says,
"to tear down institutions and inflame hatreds."
Biden also writes Trump's years of lies
about the 2020 election defeat
and the January 6th attacks on the Capitol
should, in his words, follow him to his grave.
Joe Biden's sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt
of "Promise Me, America,"
published this week by The Atlantic.
The full memoir is set for release on November 17th.
The former president also revealed
his promotional appearances will be limited.
I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Congressional Republicans meet privately to elect new House leadership after losing majority
Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan compete to replace Speaker Mike Johnson as minority leader
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth condemns impeachment effort, framing it as an attack on troops
Global Carbon Project study finds fossil fuel emissions to drop in 2026, driven by Iran war
Researchers claim chemical traces of dinosaur blood in 115-million-year-old bone
Former President Joe Biden's memoir excerpt condemns Donald Trump's damage to the country
